**Trade deals that cut the duty here:** [ASEAN–India FTA](http://localhost:8040/fta/asean-india-fta) · [GSTP (few goods)](http://localhost:8040/fta/gstp)

## HS codes covered

- [HS 100630: Rice (semi-milled or wholly milled)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/100630-rice-semi-milled-or-wholly-milled)
- [HS 100640: Rice (broken)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/100640-rice-broken)
## Export policy and registrations as of November 2026

Rice policy has changed often since 2022, so check the DGFT notifications page before each new contract.
- **IEC** from DGFT and **RCMC from APEDA**, which DGFT lists as the body for cereals.
- **Contract registration (RCAC):** upload the LC, contract or proforma invoice on the APEDA site and get an RCAC before shipment. Customs asks for it. The RCAC is valid for shipment within 45 days of issue. For non-basmati the fee is ₹8 per tonne plus GST, minimum ₹50 (APEDA trade notice, 25 September 2025); for basmati it is ₹70 per tonne plus GST (APEDA trade notice, 1 October 2025).
- **Basmati conditions:** grains must be longer than 6.61 mm with a length-to-breadth ratio above 3.5, and basmati may not be exported on documents-against-acceptance (D/A) terms unless a bank guarantee or ECGC cover backs the sale.
- **Broken rice:** DGFT moved it from Prohibited to Free on 7 March 2025 (Notification 61/2024-25). It is covered by the September 2025 contract-registration condition.
- **Europe:** under DGFT Notification 07/2026-27 of 10 April 2026, rice to EU member states, the UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland needs a Certificate of Inspection from EIC or EIA, which you upload with the RCAC application. The six-month exemption for other European countries ran until 1 October 2026, and DGFT had not published an extension by 30 October 2026, so check with EIC or APEDA before shipping rice anywhere in Europe.
- **US and China:** only from mills registered with the Directorate of Plant Protection, Quarantine and Storage. **Saudi Arabia:** only from establishments with ISO 22000 or HACCP; merchant exporters must show a certificate from the SFDA-accredited mill.
- **Indonesia, Russia and Iran** need pre-shipment testing or inspection by approved labs, as listed in the APEDA trade notice.
## Quality, testing and compliance by market

**EU and UK:** pesticide limits are strict. The EU limit for the fungicide tricyclazole in rice is 0.01 mg/kg, and basmati shipments have been rejected for residues. Work with farmers on spray schedules, and test every lot at an accredited lab.
**US:** besides mill registration with plant quarantine, the US importer must meet FDA food rules and your facility must be registered with the FDA. Pesticide residues without a US tolerance make the rice violative. Since 24 July 2026 Indian rice also pays an extra 10% US duty under Section 301; rice is not on the notice's exemption list.
**Gulf:** basmati buyers want consistent grain length, cooking quality and aged rice. Saudi Arabia's food-safety system requirement is in the APEDA notice above.
## Packaging and labelling

- Retail packs (1, 5, 10 kg) in the buyer's brand, bulk in 25 or 50 kg PP or jute bags with liners.
- Fumigation and a phytosanitary certificate where required by the destination.
- Label language, net weight, crop year and importer details as the destination requires; check private-label artwork before printing.
- Keep moisture under the contract limit; condensation in containers damages rice.
## Pricing and payment norms

Rice is quoted per tonne in US dollars, FOB Kandla, Mundra, Kakinada or other ports, or CIF. Prices track paddy prices and global competition, so validity is short. Letters of credit and cash against documents are both common; insure unsecured terms with [ECGC](http://localhost:8040/guide/ecgc-export-credit-insurance). Basmati cannot be sold on D/A terms without a bank guarantee or ECGC cover. Remember that the LC or contract you upload for the RCAC must match the shipment.
## Common mistakes

- Shipping without a valid RCAC or after it expires.
- Mixing lots with different residue profiles in one container.
- Forgetting the EIC certificate for Europe.
- Quoting long-validity prices in a market that moves weekly.
## How to start

- Get IEC and APEDA RCMC: see [RCMC](http://localhost:8040/guide/rcmc-export-promotion-council).
- Check market duty in the table below and the [import duty tool](http://localhost:8040/tools/import-duty).
- Line up a mill with the registrations your market needs (plant quarantine, ISO 22000 or HACCP).
- Sign the contract, register it with APEDA, then book freight: see [shipping and customs](http://localhost:8040/guide/export-shipping-and-customs-clearance).

**Try it on your own product:** [upload an invoice or photo](http://localhost:8040/app) to get your HS code, best countries, duty, buyers and a quote. Free.

**Exporting rice?**Tell us your product. We help with markets, buyers, documents and shipping.Ask the desk

## Questions

**Is non-basmati rice export allowed now?**

Yes. As of DGFT Notification 33/2025-26 of 24 September 2025, non-basmati rice, including broken rice, can be exported only after the contract is registered with APEDA and an RCAC is issued. Check DGFT notifications before each contract because rice policy changes often.
**What is an RCAC?**

A Registration-cum-Allocation Certificate issued by APEDA after you upload your LC, contract or proforma invoice. Customs needs it with the export documents. For non-basmati rice it is valid for shipment within 45 days of issue.
**Do I need an inspection certificate for rice to Europe?**

Yes for the EU, the UK, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. DGFT Notification 07/2026-27 of 10 April 2026 requires a Certificate of Inspection from EIC or EIA, which you upload when applying for the RCAC. Other European countries were exempt until 1 October 2026 and no extension had been published by 30 October 2026, so check before shipping.
**Can a merchant exporter sell rice to Saudi Arabia?**

Yes, but the rice must come from a mill with ISO 22000 or HACCP, and before the RCAC is issued you must upload a certificate from the SFDA-accredited establishment you bought from.

# How to export garments from India

**In short:** To export garments from India you need an IEC, an RCMC from the Apparel Export Promotion Council (AEPC), correct HS codes (chapter 61 for knits, 62 for wovens) and a factory that passes the buyer's social and chemical compliance. Labels must show fibre content, care and origin in the format each market requires. Most orders come through brands, retailers and buying houses.

Export council: **Apparel Export Promotion Council (AEPC)**
Main clusters: **Tiruppur, Ludhiana, Noida–Gurugram, Bengaluru, Jaipur**
EU fibre labelling: **Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011**
US labelling: **FTC Textile Act and Care Labeling Rule**

## What buyers abroad want and how they buy

Brands and retailers buy through their own sourcing offices or buying houses in India. They send a tech pack, then approve lab dips, fit samples, a pre-production sample and size set before bulk, and inspect the goods before shipment, usually on an AQL sampling plan.
Tiruppur is the knitwear centre (T-shirts [610910](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/610910-t-shirts-cotton-knitted-or-crocheted), polo shirts 610510, babywear [611120](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/611120-babies-garments-cotton)). Ludhiana makes sweaters (611020) and winterwear. Noida, Gurugram, Bengaluru and Jaipur make woven shirts ([620520](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/620520-men-s-shirts-boys-of-cotton)), dresses (620442) and blouses (620630). The HS code changes with knit or woven, fibre and gender, and the table below shows duty for each code in each market.

- [HS 620442: Women's suits and dresses (girls', of cotton)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/620442-women-s-suits-and-dresses-girls-of-cotton)

- [HS 611020: Sweaters and pullovers](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/611020-sweaters-and-pullovers)
## Registrations and audits

- **IEC**, **GST LUT** and **RCMC from AEPC**: see [RCMC](http://localhost:8040/guide/rcmc-export-promotion-council).
- **Social audits** that buyers commonly accept: amfori BSCI, Sedex SMETA and WRAP. Ask the buyer which one before booking.
- **Environmental and chemical programmes** for dyeing and washing units, such as ZDHC wastewater and chemical lists, are often required by large brands.
- Claim [RoDTEP and duty drawback](http://localhost:8040/guide/rodtep-and-duty-drawback) on every shipping bill.
## Compliance by market

**EU:** fibre content must be labelled using the fibre names in Regulation (EU) 1007/2011, with percentages by weight in descending order. REACH restricts azo dyes that release listed amines above 30 mg/kg in textiles that touch the skin, along with other substances. Since 13 December 2024 the General Product Safety Regulation requires an EU-based responsible operator and traceability details for consumer products; your buyer handles this, but they will ask for batch information on labels.
**UK:** the Textile Products (Labelling and Fibre Names) Regulations 2012 apply, and UK REACH carries the same azo restriction.
**US:** the FTC Textile Act requires fibre content, country of origin and the identity of the maker or seller (often an RN number), and the Care Labeling Rule requires permanent care instructions. All clothing textiles must meet the general flammability standard. Children's garments, including babywear, need third-party testing at a CPSC-accepted lab, a Children's Product Certificate from the importer and tracking labels. Since 8 July 2026 importers must e-file certificate data with US Customs at entry, so they will ask for your test reports before shipment. Since 24 July 2026 Indian garments also pay an extra 10% US duty under Section 301, on top of the normal tariff.
**Gulf and others:** requirements come mostly from the buyer's labelling and test manual. Get it before you print labels.
## Labelling, sizing and packing

- Use the buyer's size chart and grading rules; US, UK and EU sizes do not convert one-to-one.
- Main label, size label, fibre and care label (permanent, sewn in), origin "Made in India", and price or barcode tickets as the buyer specifies.
- Polybags with warnings where required, carton marks and an assortment (ratio) packing list.
- Check trims (zips, snaps, prints) for the chemical limits in the buyer's restricted substances list.
## Pricing and payment norms

Garments are quoted per piece, FOB, built from fabric consumption, trims, CMT, washing, testing, overhead and margin. Large brands mostly pay on open account 30 to 90 days after shipment, so credit insurance through [ECGC](http://localhost:8040/guide/ecgc-export-credit-insurance) matters. Smaller importers often pay an advance with the balance against documents. Use the [export price calculator](http://localhost:8040/tools/export-price-calculator).
## Common mistakes

- Using fibre names the EU list does not allow (brand names instead of the legal name).
- Skipping CPSIA testing for babywear headed to the US.
- Shrinkage and colour fastness failures discovered at final inspection.
- Accepting audit-heavy buyers before the factory's documents, wages and fire safety are in order.
## How to start

- Get IEC, GST LUT and AEPC RCMC.
- Fix HS codes with the [HS code finder](http://localhost:8040/tools/hs-code-finder) and compare duty using the table below.
- Get a recognised social audit done and keep test reports for your main fabrics.
- Meet buyers through AEPC fairs and buying houses: see [how to find export buyers](http://localhost:8040/guide/how-to-find-export-buyers).

**Try it on your own product:** [upload an invoice or photo](http://localhost:8040/app) to get your HS code, best countries, duty, buyers and a quote. Free.

**Exporting garments?**Tell us your product. We help with markets, buyers, documents and shipping.Ask the desk

## Questions

**Which export council handles readymade garments?**

The Apparel Export Promotion Council (AEPC). DGFT lists readymade garments under AEPC, so you take your RCMC from it to claim export benefits and join AEPC fairs.
**What must a garment label show for the EU?**

Fibre composition with the legal fibre names from Regulation (EU) 1007/2011 and percentages by weight. Care symbols and origin are not set by that regulation but buyers almost always require them, and some member states have their own language rules.
**Do babywear exports to the US need special testing?**

Yes. Children's products need third-party testing at a CPSC-accepted laboratory for applicable rules such as lead and, where relevant, phthalates, plus tracking labels and a Children's Product Certificate issued by the US importer or manufacturer.
**Is a BSCI or SEDEX audit a legal requirement?**

No. They are buyer requirements. But most brands and retailers will not place orders without a recognised social audit, so treat it as a condition of doing business with them.

# How to export home textiles and carpets from India

**In short:** To export home textiles from India you need an IEC and an RCMC from the right council: TEXPROCIL for cotton made-ups such as bed linen and towels, HEPC for handloom products, PDEXCIL for powerloom products, and the Carpet Export Promotion Council for handmade carpets. Buyers expect fibre labelling, chemical test reports such as OEKO-TEX, and, for carpets, proof that no child labour was used.

Councils: **TEXPROCIL, HEPC, PDEXCIL, Carpet EPC (by product and process)**
Main clusters: **Panipat, Karur, Solapur, Bhadohi–Mirzapur, Jaipur**
EU fibre labelling: **Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011**
US carpet rule: **Flammability standards for carpets and rugs (CPSC)**

## What buyers abroad want and how they buy

Home textiles are bought by retail chains, department stores, online sellers and importers who supply hotels. They order by programme (a range in several colours and sizes) and repeat if sell-through is good. Specifications cover GSM or thread count, dimensions with tolerances, shrinkage, colour fastness and packing.
Panipat makes durries, bath mats, blankets, throws and cushion covers, much of it from recycled yarn. Karur weaves table, kitchen and bed linen. Solapur is known for terry towels and chaddars. Bhadohi and Mirzapur make hand-knotted and hand-tufted carpets. Jaipur makes block-printed bedding, quilts and rugs.
Typical codes: cotton bed linen [630231](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/630231-bed-linen-and-towels-cotton), terry towels [630260](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/630260-bed-linen-and-towels-terry-towelling-or-similar-terry), furnishings 630492 and 630419, other made-ups 630790, hand-knotted carpets [570110](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/570110-hand-knotted-carpets-knotted), woven carpets 570231 and tufted carpets [570390](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/570390-tufted-carpets). The table below gives duty for each.

## HS codes covered

- [HS 630492: Furnishing articles (cotton, not knitted or crocheted)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/630492-furnishing-articles-cotton-not-knitted-or-crocheted)
- [HS 630419: Furnishing articles (not knitted or crocheted)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/630419-furnishing-articles-not-knitted-or-crocheted)

- [HS 570390: Tufted carpets](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/570390-tufted-carpets)
## Which council and registrations

- **TEXPROCIL:** cotton made-ups including bed linen, terry towels, curtains, table and kitchen linen (DGFT Appendix 2T).
- **HEPC:** all handloom products, including home furnishings, carpets and floor coverings.
- **PDEXCIL:** powerloom products.
- **Carpet Export Promotion Council (CEPC):** handmade, hand-knotted and hand-tufted carpets, rugs, durries, kelims and namdas.
- Plus **IEC**, **GST LUT** and bank AD code: see [RCMC](http://localhost:8040/guide/rcmc-export-promotion-council) for how to apply.
## Compliance by market

**EU and UK:** textile products, including bed linen and towels, need fibre content labels using the legal fibre names (Regulation (EU) 1007/2011; in the UK, the 2012 labelling regulations). REACH restricts azo dyes in textiles that touch the skin. Many buyers ask for OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certificates and, for organic claims, GOTS; these are private schemes, not laws.
**US:** the FTC Textile Act covers household textiles (fibre content, origin, maker identity), and carpets and rugs must meet CPSC flammability standards. US law (Section 307 of the Tariff Act) bars goods made with forced or indentured child labour, and CBP can detain them. The US Labor Department's list of goods produced with child or forced labour includes carpets from India. Since 24 July 2026 Indian home textiles and carpets also pay an extra 10% US duty under Section 301, on top of the normal tariff.
**Carpets and child labour:** buyers in the EU and US commonly ask for certification such as GoodWeave, plus records of weavers and sub-contractors. The EU Forced Labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 will apply from 14 December 2027.
**Gulf:** buyers focus on specification and price; agree labels and tests in the order.
## Packaging and labelling

- Retail packs with insert cards, size and fibre labels, care instructions and barcodes as the buyer specifies.
- Towels and linen sold by weight or GSM need weight tolerances agreed in the contract.
- Carpets rolled with polythene and hessian or boxed, with the size and knot or tuft details on the label.
- Wool carpets need moth protection that the destination allows; check the buyer's restricted substances list.
## Pricing and payment norms

Made-ups are quoted per piece or set, carpets per square foot or square metre, usually FOB. Cotton yarn prices move, so state a validity date. Large retailers work on open account; smaller importers pay an advance with balance against documents. See [payment terms](http://localhost:8040/guide/letter-of-credit-and-payment-terms) and [ECGC cover](http://localhost:8040/guide/ecgc-export-credit-insurance).
## Common mistakes

- Joining the wrong council, which delays your RCMC and incentive claims.
- Shipping towels that miss GSM or size tolerance.
- Unmapped sub-contracted weaving that cannot prove it is free of child labour.
- Calling a blend "100% cotton" or using non-legal fibre names on EU labels.
## How to start

- Decide your product and process, then register with the matching council.
- Confirm HS codes with the [HS code finder](http://localhost:8040/tools/hs-code-finder) and check duty in the table below.
- Get OEKO-TEX or the tests your target buyers ask for; for carpets, map your weaving network.
- Find buyers at council fairs: see [how to find export buyers](http://localhost:8040/guide/how-to-find-export-buyers).

## Questions

**Which council should a Panipat home textile exporter join?**

It depends on the product and how it is made. Cotton made-ups go to TEXPROCIL, handloom products to HEPC, powerloom products to PDEXCIL, and handmade carpets to the Carpet Export Promotion Council, as listed in DGFT Appendix 2T.
**Is OEKO-TEX certification compulsory?**

No. OEKO-TEX Standard 100 is a private certification. The legal rules are chemical restrictions like REACH, but many European buyers use OEKO-TEX as their proof, so it often decides whether you get the order.
**Why do carpet buyers ask for child-labour certification?**

US law bars goods made with forced or indentured child labour, the US Labor Department lists Indian carpets among goods at risk, and the EU Forced Labour Regulation applies from 14 December 2027. Certification such as GoodWeave and weaver records help buyers show due diligence.
**Do carpets need fire testing for the US?**

Yes. Carpets and rugs sold in the US must meet CPSC flammability standards. Your buyer will usually ask for a test report from an accredited lab for each construction.

# How to export brass, metal ware and wooden handicrafts from India

**In short:** To export brass, metal ware and wooden handicrafts from India you need an IEC and an RCMC from the Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts (EPCH). Then meet the buyer's rules on lead in coatings, food-contact safety for kitchenware and timber legality for wood. For wooden furniture sold into the EU, the Deforestation Regulation applies from 30 December 2026 for most importers. Breakage-proof packing decides your claims.

Export council: **Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts (EPCH)**
Main clusters: **Moradabad (brass, metal), Saharanpur (wood), Jodhpur (furniture), Aligarh (hardware)**
EUDR application: **30 Dec 2026 (large, medium, and small firms already under EUTR); 30 Jun 2027 (other micro, small)**
US lead in paint: **Max 90 ppm on furniture and children's items**

## What buyers abroad want and how they buy

Handicraft buyers are importers, home-décor chains, department stores and online sellers. Many first meet suppliers at EPCH's IHGF Delhi Fair, then order from a catalogue or develop designs with you. Orders are by item and finish, often with a mixed container across many items.
Moradabad makes brass and other metal artware, lamps and tableware ([741980](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/741980-brass-and-copper-articles-thereof-in-chapter-74) for copper-alloy articles) and steel kitchenware ([732393](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/732393-steel-kitchenware-table)). Saharanpur is known for carved wood, Jodhpur for wooden furniture ([940360](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/940360-furniture-wooden-other-than-for-office)), and Aligarh for locks and hardware. The table below shows duty for these codes.
## Best markets and the duty Indian goods pay

landed cost, documents and buyers.

| [Brass and copper articles (thereof in chapter 74)](http://localhost:8040/export/741980-brass-and-copper-articles-thereof-in-chapter-74/poland) HS 741980 | Poland | **3.77%** | 3.77% |
| [Brass and copper articles (thereof in chapter 74)](http://localhost:8040/export/741980-brass-and-copper-articles-thereof-in-chapter-74/united-states) HS 741980 | United States | **13%**† | 3% |
| [Brass and copper articles (thereof in chapter 74)](http://localhost:8040/export/741980-brass-and-copper-articles-thereof-in-chapter-74/united-kingdom) HS 741980 | United Kingdom | **0%** | 0% |

## HS codes covered

- [HS 741980: Brass and copper articles (thereof in chapter 74)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/741980-brass-and-copper-articles-thereof-in-chapter-74)
- [HS 732393: Steel kitchenware (table)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/732393-steel-kitchenware-table)
- [HS 940360: Furniture (wooden, other than for office)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/940360-furniture-wooden-other-than-for-office)
## Registrations you need

- **IEC**, **GST LUT** and **RCMC from EPCH**, which DGFT lists for art metal ware, wood ware and other handicrafts: see [RCMC](http://localhost:8040/guide/rcmc-export-promotion-council).
- If you make industrial stainless steel kitchenware rather than handicrafts, check DGFT Appendix 2T to confirm whether your product sits with EPCH or EEPC India.
- Keep timber purchase records and transit passes for every wooden order; buyers need them for legality checks.
## Quality, testing and compliance by market

**Lead and coatings:** in the US, paint and similar coatings with more than 90 ppm lead are banned on furniture and on toys and children's articles. Many US buyers also ask for California Proposition 65 compliance, which matters for brass because brass alloys often contain lead. In the EU, REACH limits lead in articles that children can put in their mouths. Ask your lacquer and paint suppliers for test reports.
**Food contact:** kitchenware sold in the EU must meet Regulation (EC) 1935/2004, which says materials must not transfer substances into food that endanger health. German buyers commonly ask for LFGB migration tests. Unlined brass and copper should not touch acidic food, so tableware is usually tin-lined, stainless-lined or sold as decorative only.
**Wood:** the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) covers wood and wooden furniture. According to the European Commission, it applies from 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators, and for micro and small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation (which included wooden furniture); other micro and small operators follow on 30 June 2027. Your EU buyer will ask for the geolocation of the forest or plantation and proof of legal harvest. FSC certification helps but does not replace this. The US Lacey Act also makes importing illegally harvested wood an offence. Sheesham (Dalbergia sissoo) is still listed under CITES. Since a 2022 change, items in which the sheesham wood weighs under 10 kg each can ship without CITES permits; heavier pieces such as beds and dining tables still need them. Confirm the current rule with EPCH before quoting.
**Wooden packaging** must be ISPM-15 treated and marked for most destinations.
## Packaging and breakage

- Pack to the buyer's drop and vibration test standard; e-commerce buyers often require ISTA testing.
- Use moulded pulp, corner protectors and double-wall cartons; wrap polished brass in acid-free paper so it does not tarnish.
- Kiln-dry wood to the moisture level the buyer specifies and use desiccants to stop mould and cracking in the container.
- Label each carton with item code, quantity and "Made in India"; the US requires origin marking on the article itself where possible.
## Pricing and payment norms

Quote per piece FOB, with metal, wood and finish costed separately, and state the minimum per item and per container. Samples are usually charged. Smaller importers often pay an advance with the balance against documents; large chains may want open account. Use the [export price calculator](http://localhost:8040/tools/export-price-calculator) and read [Incoterms](http://localhost:8040/guide/incoterms-for-indian-exporters).
For the US, most Indian goods have paid an extra 10% duty under Section 301 since 24 July 2026. Steel, copper and wood products that already pay US Section 232 tariffs are excluded from it but pay those instead, so ask the importer's customs broker which applies to each item before quoting.
## Common mistakes

- Lacquers or paints bought on price with no lead test report.
- Selling decorative brass as food-safe tableware.
- No timber legality paperwork when an EU buyer asks for EUDR data.
- Packing that passes in the factory but fails a drop test, leading to breakage claims.
## How to start

- Get IEC, GST LUT and EPCH RCMC.
- Fix HS codes with the [HS code finder](http://localhost:8040/tools/hs-code-finder) and compare duty in the table below.
- Get lead and food-contact tests for your main finishes and organise timber records.
- Exhibit or visit EPCH fairs and contact buyers: see [how to find export buyers](http://localhost:8040/guide/how-to-find-export-buyers).

**Try it on your own product:** [upload an invoice or photo](http://localhost:8040/app) to get your HS code, best countries, duty, buyers and a quote. Free.

**Exporting brass, metal ware and wooden handicrafts?**Tell us your product. We help with markets, buyers, documents and shipping.Ask the desk

## Questions

**Which council should a Moradabad brass exporter join?**

The Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts (EPCH). DGFT's list of councils assigns art metal ware, wood ware and other handicrafts to EPCH, and it runs the IHGF Delhi Fair where many buyers first meet suppliers.
**When does the EU Deforestation Regulation apply to wooden furniture?**

The European Commission states it applies from 30 December 2026 for large and medium operators and for micro and small operators already covered by the EU Timber Regulation, and from 30 June 2027 for other micro and small operators. Wooden furniture is covered, so EU buyers will ask for plot geolocation and legality proof.
**Can I sell brass utensils as food-safe?**

Only if they are lined or tested for the market. The EU requires food-contact materials not to transfer harmful substances into food, and buyers ask for migration tests. Unlined brass and copper are usually sold as decorative.
**What lead limit applies to painted furniture in the US?**

US rules ban paint and similar surface coatings containing more than 90 ppm lead on furniture for consumer use and on toys and children's articles. Get test reports for each paint or lacquer you use.

## Official sources

- [Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts](https://www.epch.in/)
- [DGFT: Appendix 2T, export promotion councils](https://content.dgft.gov.in/Website/dgftprod/3020e31a-d8b5-480d-b099-809d219b9020/APPENDIX%202T%20as%20on%2006.02.2023.pdf)

# How to export shrimp and frozen seafood from India

**In short:** To export shrimp from India you need an IEC, registration as an exporter with MPEDA, and a processing plant approved by the Export Inspection Council (EIC) for markets such as the EU, which issues the health certificate. Every lot must be free of banned antibiotics. In the US, Indian shrimp faces anti-dumping and countervailing duties plus, since 24 July 2026, a 10% Section 301 duty, and only farmed shrimp can enter.

Export body: **MPEDA (registration); EIC (plant approval, health certificates)**
Main hubs: **Andhra Pradesh (Bhimavaram, Nellore), Kochi, Gujarat**
US trade remedies: **Anti-dumping order since 2005; countervailing order since Dec 2024**
US Section 609: **Only farmed shrimp from India eligible; DS-2031 with every shipment**

## What buyers abroad want and how they buy

Most Indian shrimp is farmed vannamei from Andhra Pradesh, processed into frozen headless shell-on, peeled, deveined or cooked forms. Buyers are importers, retail chains and food-service distributors who buy by count per pound or kilo, glaze percentage, net weight and processing style, and who audit the plant.
Frozen shrimp is HS [030617](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/030617-shrimp-and-prawns-frozen); Kochi and Gujarat exporters also ship cuttlefish and squid (030743), frozen fish (030389) and fish meat (030499). The table below shows the normal duty in each market and what trade deals change; US trade-remedy duties are explained here instead.
## Best markets and the duty Indian goods pay

## HS codes covered

- [HS 030617: Shrimp and prawns (frozen)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/030617-shrimp-and-prawns-frozen)
- [HS 030743: Squid and molluscs (cuttle fish whether in shell or not, frozen)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/030743-squid-and-molluscs-cuttle-fish-whether-in-shell-or-not)
- [HS 030389: Frozen fish (in heading 0303, excluding fillets, meat of 0304)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/030389-frozen-fish-in-heading-0303-excluding-fillets-meat-of-0304)
- [HS 030499: Fish fillets (frozen)](http://localhost:8040/hs-code/030499-fish-fillets-frozen)
## Registrations and approvals

- **IEC** from DGFT and **registration as an exporter with MPEDA**, which DGFT lists as the body for marine products and which serves as your RCMC.
- **EIC approval of the processing plant** for the EU and other markets that require it. Approved Indian plants appear on the EU's list of establishments; you cannot ship to the EU from an unlisted plant.
- **Export health certificate** issued by EIC's agencies for each consignment where the importing country requires it.
- **US FDA food facility registration** for the plant, renewed between 1 October and 31 December of even years, and a seafood HACCP plan.
- **China** requires the overseas manufacturer to be registered with its customs authority before export.
## Antibiotics and testing by market

**EU:** residues of banned antibiotics such as nitrofurans and chloramphenicol lead to border rejections. From 3 September 2026 the EU also requires that farmed animals, including aquaculture shrimp, were not given antimicrobials for growth promotion or antimicrobials reserved for human use; the exporting country must be on the EU's commodity-specific list and the health certificate carries this attestation. Confirm with EIC that your product is covered before contracting.
**US:** importers must verify that the foreign processor follows FDA's seafood HACCP rules, and FDA can detain shipments found with unapproved drugs. Shrimp is also covered by NOAA's Seafood Import Monitoring Program, under which the US importer reports harvest data for each shipment, so keep pond and harvest records for every lot. Use only hatcheries and farms with residue testing records.
**Everywhere:** test raw material before processing; EIC runs India's residue monitoring for aquaculture, but buyers expect your own lot testing too.
## US duties and Section 609, as verified on 3 November 2026

- **Anti-dumping duty:** an order on frozen warmwater shrimp from India has been in place since 2005. Rates are company-specific and reset in annual reviews; the latest final results (for February 2024 to January 2025) were published on 4 September 2026.
- **Countervailing duty:** an order on Indian shrimp was issued in December 2024. Rates are also company-specific.
- **Section 301:** under USTR's notice of 23 July 2026 (Federal Register, 28 July 2026), products of India entered on or after 24 July 2026 pay an additional 10% on top of the normal duty, except goods on the notice's exemption list (Annex II, Part A). Frozen shrimp (HTS 0306.17) is not on that list, so the 10% applies, and anti-dumping and countervailing duties continue on top. A separate Section 301 investigation on excess capacity, which includes India, had no announced action when we checked.
- **Section 609 (sea turtles):** India is not certified, so only shrimp from aquaculture can enter the US. Every shipment must carry the DS-2031 declaration.
- The US importer pays these duties at entry, so they come straight out of your price. Agree who bears later rate changes in the contract.
## Packaging and labelling

- Declare net weight after glaze; over-glazing is treated as short weight.
- Carton labels with species name, count, net weight, plant approval number, production date, lot and "Product of India".
- Cold chain at -18°C or colder, with temperature logs from plant to port.
## Pricing, payment, common mistakes and how to start

Shrimp is quoted per kg or per pound by count, usually CFR or CIF. Letters of credit and documents against payment are common; open account with large US importers carries risk, so use [ECGC](http://localhost:8040/guide/ecgc-export-credit-insurance). Common mistakes: shipping from a plant not on the EU list, missing DS-2031 forms, buying farm shrimp without residue records, and quoting US prices without allowing for anti-dumping, countervailing and Section 301 duties.
- Get IEC and MPEDA registration; apply to EIC for plant approval.
- Register the plant with the US FDA and build a seafood HACCP plan if you will sell to the US.
- Check market duty in the table below and the [import duty tool](http://localhost:8040/tools/import-duty).
- Find buyers: see [how to find export buyers](http://localhost:8040/guide/how-to-find-export-buyers).

**Try it on your own product:** [upload an invoice or photo](http://localhost:8040/app) to get your HS code, best countries, duty, buyers and a quote. Free.

## Questions

**Is MPEDA registration compulsory for shrimp exporters?**

Yes. Exporters of marine products must register with MPEDA, which DGFT lists as the body for marine products. The registration also serves as the RCMC you need for export benefits.
**Can Indian wild-caught shrimp be exported to the US?**

No. India is not certified under Section 609 of US law on sea-turtle protection, so only farmed shrimp is eligible. Every shrimp shipment, farmed or wild, must carry the DS-2031 declaration.
**What extra US duties apply to Indian shrimp?**

As verified on 3 November 2026: company-specific anti-dumping and countervailing duties, plus a 10% Section 301 duty on Indian goods entered from 24 July 2026. Check USTR and Federal Register notices before quoting, as these change.
**Do I need EIC approval to export shrimp to the EU?**

Yes. The processing plant must be approved by EIC and appear on the EU list of approved establishments, and each consignment needs a health certificate. From 3 September 2026 the certificate also carries the EU antimicrobial-use attestation.
**Do EU rules on antibiotics affect farmers or only processors?**

Both. The EU rules from 3 September 2026 cover how the shrimp was raised, so processors need records from hatcheries and farms showing no growth-promoting or reserved antimicrobials were used.
